parts.latex: Which interval gives the range of the function $y=5+2\cos 3x$?

solutions.latex:
Start from the range of cosine, then build up $y$ one step at a time:
$$\begin{aligned} -1&\le \cos 3x\le 1\\ -2&\le 2\cos 3x\le 2 &&(\text{multiply by } 2)\\ 3&\le 5+2\cos 3x\le 7 &&(\text{add } 5)\end{aligned}$$
So $3\le y\le 7$: the range is $[3,7]$.

parts.latex: For what values of $x$, in the interval $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, does the line $y=1$ intersect the graph of $y=2\sin 4x$?

solutions.latex:
Since $0 \le x \le \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, then $0 \le 4x \le \pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin 4x &= 1 \\ \sin 4x &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 4x &= \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{\pi}{24},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{24} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=\sin(2x)$.

Find the value of $x$, for $0<x<\pi$, for which $f'(x)=-\sqrt{3}$ AND $f''(x)=2$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \sin 2x \\ f'(x) &= 2\cos 2x \\ f''(x) &= -4\sin 2x \end{aligned}$$
When $f'(x) = -\sqrt{3}$,
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos 2x &= -\sqrt{3} \\ \cos 2x &= \dfrac{-\sqrt{3}}{2} \qquad 0 < 2x < 2\pi \\ 2x &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
When $f''(x) = 2$,
$$\begin{aligned} -4\sin 2x &= 2 \\ \sin 2x &= \dfrac{-1}{2} \qquad 0 < 2x < 2\pi \\ 2x &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \text{ for } 0 < x < \pi$$
criteria: Finds the values of $x$, $0 < x < \pi$, for each derivative equation
Attempts to find a value for $x$ that solves $f'(x)$ or $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The function $f(x)=\sqrt{3}\cos(\alpha-2x)$ is odd. Its graph also increases in the interval of $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. What is a possible value of $\alpha$?

solutions.latex:
Since $f$ is odd, $f(0) = \sqrt{3}\cos\alpha = 0$, so $\cos\alpha = 0$.

$\therefore$ eliminate B and C.

If $\alpha = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \sqrt{3}\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2x\right) \\ &= \sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+2x\right) \\ &= -\sqrt{3}\sin 2x \end{aligned}$$
which decreases on $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (sketch).

If $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2x\right) \\ &= \sqrt{3}\sin 2x \end{aligned}$$
which increases on $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (sketch).

$\therefore\ \alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

parts.latex:
Consider the function $f(x)=k\cos\left(6x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+c$, where $c$ and $k$ are constants.

The function has a minimum value of $-1$ and a maximum value of $5$.

Which row of the table shows the correct amplitude, period and phase?

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is half the distance between the maximum and minimum:
$$\text{Amplitude} = \dfrac{5 - (-1)}{2} = 3$$
The period of $\cos 6x$ is
$$\dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
For the phase, factor the $6$ out of the angle:
$$6x + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 6\left(x + \dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)$$
so the phase is $\dfrac{\pi}{12}$.

parts.latex: Determine the values of $x$ for which the graph of $y=3\cos\left(\dfrac{5x-1}{2}\right)$ crosses the $x$-axis in the interval $0\le x\le\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Solve for $x$ when $y=0$:

$$\begin{aligned}3\cos\left(\dfrac{5x-1}{2}\right)&=0\\ \cos\left(\dfrac{5x-1}{2}\right)&=0\\ \left(\dfrac{5x-1}{2}\right)&=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{5\pi}{2},\ldots\\ 5x-1&=\pi,3\pi,5\pi,\ldots\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi+1}{5},\ \dfrac{3\pi+1}{5}$$
criteria: Provides one correct solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the period of the function $y=4\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)$?

solutions.latex:
For $y = a\sin(bx)$ the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$. Here $b = \dfrac{1}{3}$, so the period is
$$\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{1}{3}} = 6\pi$$

parts.latex: Find the equations of the vertical asymptotes on the curve $y=\tan\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
$x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}=m\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $m$ an odd integer such that
$$\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le m\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le 2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$

$\therefore\ m=1,3$

Vertical asymptotes have equations $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. writes the equation of one asymptote

parts.latex: Determine the values of $x$ for which the graph of $y=3\cos\left(\dfrac{5x-1}{2}\right)$ crosses the $x$-axis in the interval $0\le x\le\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Solve for $x$ when $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3\cos\left(\dfrac{5x-1}{2}\right)&=0\\ \cos\left(\dfrac{5x-1}{2}\right)&=0\\ \left(\dfrac{5x-1}{2}\right)&=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{5\pi}{2},\ldots\\ 5x-1&=\pi,3\pi,5\pi,\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi+1}{5},\ \dfrac{3\pi+1}{5}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following functions best represents the graph below? \exfigure{1365_q9_1}

solutions.latex:
From the graph, the asymptotes are $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ apart, so the period is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

For $y=\tan(nx)$ the period is $\dfrac{\pi}{n}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{n}&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\ n&=2 \end{aligned}$$
The graph is $y=\tan 2x$ shifted $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ to the left:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \tan\left(2\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right) \\ &= \tan\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Write the equation for a sound wave $P_1(t)$ that has an amplitude of 2 Pascals and a period of 5 ms.
Hence, find the values of $t$, where $0<t<10$, for which functions $P_1(t)$ and $P_2(t)$ are BOTH decreasing.

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is 2, so
$$k=2$$
The period is 5 ms:
$$\dfrac{2\pi}{a}=5$$
$$a=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$$
$$\therefore\ P_1(t)=2\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{5}t$$

criteria: Draws a sine wave with an amplitude of 4, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From the graphs ($P_1$ decreases from each maximum to the next minimum):
$$\begin{aligned} &P_2 \text{ decreasing} &&\text{for } 5<t<10\\ &P_1 \text{ decreasing} &&\text{for } 1.25<t<3.75 \text{ and } 6.25<t<8.75\end{aligned}$$
Only $6.25<t<8.75$ lies inside $5<t<10$, so both are decreasing for
$$6.25<t<8.75$$
criteria: Finds one correct endpoint of interval, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The equation $\cos px=\dfrac{1}{2}$ has 2 solutions where $0\le x\le 2\pi$ and $p>0$.

Find all possible values of $p$.

solutions.latex:
Solve $\cos x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $x\ge 0$ first:
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \ldots$$
\exfigure{1630_q31_s1}

$y=\cos px$ is a horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{p}$, so its solutions are these values multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{p}$.

Lowest value of $p$ to get 2 solutions (second solution at $x=2\pi$):

\exfigure{1630_q31_s2}
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{p} &= 2\pi \\ p &= \dfrac{5\pi}{3\times 2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Highest value of $p$ (at this value a third solution appears at $x=2\pi$, so it is excluded):

\exfigure{1630_q31_s3}
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{7\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{p} &= 2\pi \\ p &= \dfrac{7\pi}{3\times 2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{7}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{5}{6}\le p<\dfrac{7}{6}$$

parts.latex: Find the range and period of the function $h(x)=3\cos(2x)+1$.

solutions.latex:
Range: since $-1\le\cos(2x)\le 1$,
$$\begin{aligned} -1&\le \cos(2x)\le 1\\ -3&\le 3\cos(2x)\le 3 &&(\text{multiply by } 3)\\ -2&\le 3\cos(2x)+1\le 4 &&(\text{add } 1)\end{aligned}$$
So the range is $-2\le h(x)\le 4$.

Period: for $\cos(nx)$ the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$, with $n=2$:
$$\text{period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$$
criteria: Finds the correct range or the correct period, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following correctly describes the order of the transformations of $y=\sin x$ to $y=3\sin(2x-1)$?

solutions.latex:
Order of transformations from $y=f(x)$ to $y=kf(a(x+b))+c$:

\begin{itemize}
\item Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{a}$
\item Translate $b$ units left
\item Dilate vertically by a factor of $k$
\item Translate up $c$ units
\end{itemize}

Write the equation in this form:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3\sin(2x-1)\\&=3\sin\left(2\left(x-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The transformations are, in order:

\begin{itemize}
\item Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$
\item Horizontal translation right $\dfrac{1}{2}$
\item Vertical dilation by a factor of 3
\end{itemize}

parts.latex:
The function $y = 2\sin x + 1$ is translated up $m$ units and then vertically dilated by a factor of $n$ from the $x$-axis, where $m$ and $n$ are positive numbers.

What is the range of the new curve?

solutions.latex:
Translating up $m$ units:
$$y = 2\sin x + m + 1$$
Dilating vertically by a factor of $n$:
$$y = 2n\sin x + mn + n$$
The amplitude is $2n$ and the centre is $y = mn + n$, so the range is
$$[mn + n - 2n,\ mn + n + 2n] = [mn - n,\ mn + 3n]$$

parts.latex: Solve $2\cos 2x=\sqrt{3}$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Dividing by 2:
$$\cos 2x=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
Adjusting the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} -\pi &\le x \le \pi \\ -2\pi &\le 2x \le 2\pi &&(\text{multiply by } 2) \end{aligned}$$
The related acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ (cosine is positive in quadrants 1 and 4).

\exfigure{644_q9_s1}
$$\begin{aligned} 2x &= \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\left(2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{11\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12},\ -\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ -\dfrac{11\pi}{12}$$
criteria: Finds all four values $2x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pm\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ in $-2\pi\le 2x\le 2\pi$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following function has a period of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and is increasing in the domain $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$?

solutions.latex:
$|\cos(2x)|$ has period $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

On the given domain:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{4}&<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\ \dfrac{\pi}{2}&<2x<\pi &&(\text{multiply by } 2)\end{aligned}$$
so $\cos(2x)$ is negative and decreasing, hence $|\cos(2x)|$ is increasing.

parts.latex: Solve for $x$ where $0\le x\le 2\pi$, $\quad\operatorname{cosec}\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\sqrt{2}$

solutions.latex:
Since $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)}&=\sqrt{2}\\ \sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
Adjusting the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le x\le 2\pi\\ \dfrac{\pi}{3}&\le x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le\dfrac{7\pi}{3} &&\left(\text{add } \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{4} &&\text{(invalid)}\\ &=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{9\pi}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{11\pi}{4} &&\text{(invalid)}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ x&=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ or } \dfrac{9\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{5\pi}{12} \text{ or } \dfrac{23\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct angles in the shifted domain, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Prove

$$\dfrac{\sec^2(2\theta)}{\sec^2(2\theta)-1}=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta).$$
Hence, solve $\dfrac{\sec^2(2\theta)}{\sec^2(2\theta)-1}=2$ where $0\le\theta\le\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\sec^2(2\theta)=\tan^2(2\theta)+1$, so that $\sec^2(2\theta)-1=\tan^2(2\theta)$, and $1+\cot^2(2\theta)=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\tan^2(2\theta)+1}{\tan^2(2\theta)} \\ &=1+\dfrac{1}{\tan^2(2\theta)} \\ &=1+\cot^2(2\theta) \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta) \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, writing $\sec$ in terms of $\cos$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\cos^2(2\theta)}}{\frac{1}{\cos^2(2\theta)}-1} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\cos^2(2\theta)}}{\frac{1-\cos^2(2\theta)}{\cos^2(2\theta)}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\cos^2(2\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2(2\theta)} \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta) \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses trigonometric identities to simplify the LHS to $1+\dfrac{1}{\tan^2 2\theta}$ or $\dfrac{1}{1-\cos^2 2\theta}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le\theta\le\pi \\ 0&\le2\theta\le2\pi &&(\text{multiply by } 2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta)&=2 \\ \operatorname{cosec}(2\theta)&=\pm\sqrt{2} \\ \sin(2\theta)&=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so in $0\le2\theta\le2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \\ \theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{8} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given $\sin^2 x=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x$ and using only translations, reflections and dilations, carefully state all of the transformations required to transform the function $y=\sin x$ to obtain the function $y=\sin^2 x$.

solutions.latex:
First, $y=\cos x$ is $y=\sin x$ translated horizontally to the left by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, since $\cos x=\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

Next, $y=\cos(2x)$ is $y=\cos x$ with a horizontal compression by a factor of $2$.

Then, $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x)$ is $y=\cos(2x)$ with a reflection in the $x$-axis and a vertical compression by a factor of $2$.

Finally, $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x)$ is $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x)$ with a vertical translation of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ upwards.

parts.latex: A cosine function $f$ has a maximum value of $2$, a minimum value of $-1$, and a period of $\dfrac{2}{5}$. The function could be:

solutions.latex:
The maximum is $2$ and the minimum is $-1$, so the amplitude and the centre line are
$$\begin{aligned} \text{amplitude} &= \dfrac{2-(-1)}{2}=1.5 \\ \text{centre} &= \dfrac{2+(-1)}{2}=0.5 \end{aligned}$$
The period is $\dfrac{2}{5}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2\pi}{n} &= \dfrac{2}{5} \\ n &= 5\pi \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore f(x)=1.5\cos(5\pi x)+0.5$, which is option D.

For $0\le x\le\pi$ we need $0\le 2x\le 2\pi$.

Since $\tan 2x=\sqrt{3}$ and tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants,
$$2x=\dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ or } \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ or } \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$$
